title: Diagnosing a port that is not reachable
description: Systematically diagnose why a TCP or UDP port is unreachable.

data.text: A port that is not reachable is one of the most common production issues. Users report timeouts, health checks fail, and deployments cannot reach databases. The cause could be that nothing is listening on the port, a firewall is blocking it, the service is bound to the wrong address, or the process has crashed.

Port diagnosis is a step-by-step process. Start from the server and work outward: Is the process running? Is it listening on the expected port? Is the firewall allowing the traffic? Is the network path clear? Each step eliminates a category of problems.

The first question is whether the process that should be listening on the port is actually running. Use systemctl status or ps aux to confirm. If the process is not running, start it and check its logs for startup errors.

data.code:
systemctl status nginx
ps aux | grep nginx
journalctl -u nginx --since "10 min ago"

data.text: Use ss to see if the process is listening on the expected port and address. Pay attention to the Local Address column. If the service binds to 127.0.0.1, it is only reachable from the same machine. If it binds to 0.0.0.0, it is reachable from any network interface.

data.code:
ss -tulnp | grep :8080
# LISTEN 0 128 0.0.0.0:8080 ... means reachable from outside
# LISTEN 0 128 127.0.0.1:8080 ... means localhost only

data.text: Linux firewalls use iptables, nftables, or firewalld. Even if a service is listening, a firewall rule can block incoming connections. Check the active firewall rules for the port. On cloud servers, a cloud firewall or security group may also be blocking the traffic.

data.code:
sudo iptables -L -n | grep 8080
sudo firewall-cmd --list-all
# On AWS, check the security group in the console

data.title: Security groups matter
data.text: Cloud providers often have a separate firewall outside the server. If iptables shows the port is open but you still cannot connect, check the cloud console for security group or network ACL rules. This is a common oversight.

From the client machine, use nc or curl to test connectivity. nc with the -z flag checks if a port is open without sending data. If nc fails but the server shows the port open, the problem is in the network path: routing, VPN, or an intermediate firewall.

items: Confirm the process is running with systemctl or ps
Confirm the port is listening with ss
Check local firewall rules with iptables or firewalld
Check cloud security groups if applicable
Test from the client with nc or curl

data.title: Key Takeaways
items: Start from the server and work outward when diagnosing ports
ss shows listening ports and their bind addresses
Firewalls and cloud security groups can block reachable ports
nc tests TCP connectivity without sending application data
Bind address matters: 127.0.0.1 is localhost only
